title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
When I first encountered the Transformer, the diagram looked more complicated than the idea behind it. The useful starting question was simple: **when a model processes one token, how can it decide which other tokens are relevant?**

Attention gives it a learned way to combine information from different positions. The Transformer builds a sequence model around that operation, together with positional information, feed-forward layers, and connections that make a deep network trainable.

This guide moves from that intuition to a small implementation. You do not need to memorize the full architecture before understanding what happens inside one attention head.

> Reading goal: explain what Q, K, and V do, trace the shape of an attention calculation, and understand why a decoder needs a causal mask.

## 1. The problem the paper addressed

Earlier sequence models often used recurrent networks. A recurrent layer carries state from one position to the next, which creates a dependency along the sequence. Attention already existed in sequence-to-sequence systems; the 2017 paper did not introduce the first attention mechanism.

[Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), by Vaswani and colleagues, introduced the Transformer architecture for sequence transduction without recurrence or convolution in its core sequence-processing blocks. The original model had an encoder and a decoder and was evaluated on tasks including machine translation.

The distinction matters: the original translation architecture and a modern decoder-only language model share important building blocks, but they are not identical systems.

### Why parallelism changed training

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
During Transformer training, many positions can be processed together through matrix operations. A causal mask can prevent access to future targets while still allowing parallel computation over the supplied sequence.

Autoregressive generation is different. To produce a new response, a model typically generates a token, appends it, and uses that result to generate the next token. Parallel training does not mean that an entire unknown response is generated in one step.

## 2. Build a small vocabulary first

| Term | Meaning in this guide |
| --- | --- |
| Token | A unit produced by a tokenizer; often a word fragment, punctuation mark, or other symbol |
| Embedding | A learned vector associated with a token |
| Hidden state | A token’s representation after processing by a layer |
| Head | One attention calculation using its own projections |
| Logits | Unnormalized scores before a softmax |
| Context window | The sequence capacity supported by a particular model and configuration |

A token is not necessarily a whole word. Also, a vector’s individual coordinates do not generally correspond to simple labels such as “animal” or “past tense.” Those labels can be useful teaching analogies, but learned representations are distributed.

## 3. Start with token representations

Suppose a sequence contains `n` tokens and each representation has `d_model` features. We can arrange those representations in a matrix:

```text
X: [n, d_model]

Each row represents one token position.
Each column is one learned feature coordinate.
```

The model also needs information about position. The original Transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings. Other architectures use different positional methods.

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
The result is a representation of token content together with positional information. Attention can then use learned projections to decide how information should move between positions.

## 4. Queries, keys, and values

For one attention head, the model projects the input into three matrices:

```text
Q = X Wq    queries: [n, d_k]
K = X Wk    keys:    [n, d_k]
V = X Wv    values:  [n, d_v]
```

A useful interpretation is:

- A **query** describes what information a position is looking for.
- A **key** provides something that can be compared with that query.
- A **value** contains information that can contribute to the output.

These are learned numerical projections. They are not literal search questions or database keys. Training adjusts the projection weights so that the operation becomes useful for the objective.

### Compare, normalize, combine

For every query, compute a dot product with the available keys. Scale those scores by the square root of the key dimension, apply any mask, then use softmax to form weights.

```text
scores  = Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)     [n, n]
weights = softmax(scores)      [n, n], normalized across keys
output  = weights V           [n, d_v]
```

Each output row is a weighted combination of value vectors. The scaling helps control the magnitude of the dot products as the dimension grows.

### A numerical example

Assume one query produces two scaled scores: `2` and `1`. Softmax turns them into approximately `0.731` and `0.269`.

```text
Scaled scores: [2, 1]
Weights:       [0.731, 0.269]

Value A:       [10, 0]
Value B:       [0, 10]

Weighted result:
0.731 × [10, 0] + 0.269 × [0, 10] ≈ [7.31, 2.69]
```

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
outputs, all_weights = [], []
    for position, query in enumerate(queries):
        count = position + 1 if causal else len(keys)
        scores = [
            sum(q * k for q, k in zip(query, key)) / math.sqrt(key_dim)
            for key in keys[:count]
        ]
        # Subtracting the maximum makes softmax more stable.
        exponentials = [math.exp(score - max(scores)) for score in scores]
        total = sum(exponentials)
        weights = [value / total for value in exponentials]
        output = [
            sum(weight * value[column]
                for weight, value in zip(weights, values[:count]))
            for column in range(value_dim)
        ]
        outputs.append(output)
        all_weights.append(weights + [0.0] * (len(keys) - count))
    return outputs, all_weights

q = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
k = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
v = [[10.0, 0.0], [0.0, 10.0]]

output, weights = attention(q, k, v, causal=True)
assert output[0] == v[0]  # The first position cannot read the second.
assert weights[0][1] == 0.0
assert all(abs(sum(row) - 1.0) < 1e-9 for row in weights)
print([[round(value, 3) for value in row] for row in output])
```

Read the assertions before changing the example. They capture two useful invariants: forbidden positions receive zero weight, and each valid attention row sums to one.

This function does not implement learned projections, batching, padding masks, dropout, or gradients. It demonstrates the attention operation after Q, K, and V have already been constructed.

## 6. Why causal masking matters

In next-token training, the model must not use a token that appears after the position it is predicting from. Otherwise, training would expose information that is unavailable during generation.

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
```text
Allowed key positions for each query position:

           key 0   key 1   key 2
query 0      yes      no      no
query 1      yes     yes      no
query 2      yes     yes     yes
```

A common tensor implementation assigns forbidden score entries negative infinity before softmax. Their resulting probability is zero. Be careful with padding: a row with no allowed keys needs explicit handling, since a softmax over only negative infinities can produce invalid values.

An encoder’s self-attention can use the full available input sequence. Decoder self-attention applies a causal constraint. In an encoder–decoder model, cross-attention uses decoder queries and encoder keys and values.

## 7. Put attention inside a Transformer block

Attention moves information between positions. A feed-forward network then transforms the representation at each position. Residual connections provide paths around sublayers, while normalization helps manage the scale of intermediate activations.

Multi-head attention performs several attention calculations with separate projections, concatenates their results, and applies an output projection. Heads can learn different useful patterns, but it is too simplistic to label every head permanently as “grammar,” “meaning,” or “pronoun resolution.”

| Architecture | Typical information flow | Common task shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder-only | Input positions can use the supplied context | Representation and classification |
| Decoder-only | Positions attend under a causal constraint | Next-token generation |
| Encoder–decoder | A decoder also attends to encoded input | Input-to-output sequence tasks |

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
Layer placement, normalization, activation functions, and positional methods vary across implementations. Learning the original block is a starting point, not a description of every model called a Transformer.

## 8. Understand training and inference separately

During next-token training, known token sequences supply the targets. The model predicts distributions over the vocabulary, and the training loss compares those predictions with the expected tokens. Optimization changes the model parameters.

During ordinary inference, those parameters stay fixed. The application selects tokens from the output distribution using a decoding strategy. Temperature and sampling affect selection; they do not teach the model new facts by updating its weights.

A key–value cache reuses previously computed keys and values during autoregressive decoding. This saves repeated work, while the stored cache consumes memory as the sequence grows. Retrieval, prompt history, and weight updates are separate mechanisms and should not all be described as “memory.”

## 9. What later improvements change

Several later techniques address different limitations. They are useful to distinguish because they do not solve the same problem.

### Rotary positional embeddings

[RoFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) describes rotary positional embeddings, commonly called RoPE. The method applies position-dependent rotations to representations used in attention, allowing relative position to affect their interaction. It is a positional method; it does not make arbitrary context lengths reliable by itself.

### FlashAttention

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
[FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) reorganizes exact attention computation to reduce costly memory traffic. It is an implementation improvement, not a replacement of attention with a different semantic operation. It does not change standard dense attention’s quadratic pairwise computation into linear computation.

### Grouped-query attention

[Grouped-query attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245), or GQA, lets groups of query heads share key and value heads. This reduces key–value storage relative to a corresponding multi-head setup and offers a useful inference tradeoff. The quality and speed of a complete model still depend on its architecture, training, and hardware.

## 10. Common misunderstandings

- **“Attention is an explanation.”** Attention weights show one internal operation. They do not automatically establish why a model produced a particular answer.
- **“More context guarantees better answers.”** A larger supported window provides capacity. Relevant retrieval, clear instructions, and evaluation still matter.
- **“Every modern language model uses the original architecture.”** Models change blocks and may use other sequence-processing designs.
- **“A tutorial’s speedup applies to my machine.”** Performance claims require a defined workload, implementation, hardware, and measurement method.

## What I would learn next

First, run the small function and inspect how its weights change when you alter a query or key. Next, implement the same operation with a tensor library and compare its output on identical inputs. Then add learned projections, multiple heads, and a padding mask.

title: Attention Is All You Need: From Intuition to Implementation
content:
That sequence makes each abstraction earn its place. The large model becomes easier to understand once you can trace how a single position collects information from the rest of a sequence.

## Further reading

- [Attention Is All You Need — original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)
- [RoFormer — rotary positional embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)
- [FlashAttention — IO-aware exact attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)
- [GQA — grouped-query attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
An AI agent can produce a convincing explanation of a feature without actually finishing it. The files may exist, yet the route is broken. A test may pass, yet the real user flow still fails. The gap is often in the system around the model: what it can inspect, how it takes actions, and what evidence counts as completion.

That surrounding system is the **harness**. It connects a model to tools, working context, execution rules, and feedback. Harness engineering means designing those connections so that progress is observable and mistakes are recoverable.

This guide follows a coding task from the first request to a verified handoff. The same ideas apply to research assistants and other tool-using workflows, although their verification steps will differ.

> A useful completion report tells you what changed, how it was checked, and what remains unresolved. Confident wording is not evidence.

## 1. Understand the model–runtime boundary

The model generates messages and may request tool calls. The runtime decides whether those calls are allowed, executes them, and returns results. Writing a shell command in a response does not execute it. Returning valid JSON does not prove that its contents are correct.

| Layer | Responsibility | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Propose an action or answer | Request a file read |
| Tool interface | Define the operation and input shape | Read one repository file |
| Runtime | Validate and execute the request | Enforce the workspace boundary |
| Verification | Check the resulting behavior | Open the route and test the interaction |
| State | Preserve decisions and evidence | Record a passing check and the next task |

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
Keeping these responsibilities separate makes failures easier to diagnose. If a file was never written, inspect the tool result. If the file exists but the feature fails, inspect the implementation and its integration.

### What a tool call actually does

Consider an assistant that needs to inspect a configuration file. A simplified request might look like this:

```json
{
  "tool": "read_file",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "package.json"
  }
}
```

The application validates the tool name and arguments, resolves the path within the permitted workspace, and returns the file contents or an explicit error. The next model turn can then use that result.

This interactive flow is a teaching model. Real providers use their own message and tool-call formats, but the important boundary stays the same: **a requested action and an executed action are different events**.

### A sandbox is an execution boundary

A sandbox limits access to resources such as files, processes, and network destinations. Its protection depends on its configuration. A workspace restriction, for example, does not automatically restrict an external database whose credentials were passed to a tool.

Give each tool the narrowest useful capability. Prefer a repository file reader over an unrestricted shell when the task only needs a file. Keep secrets out of tool output and use explicit approval for consequential external actions.

## 2. Design five connected parts

I find it useful to reason about a harness through five parts: instructions, state, verification, scope, and session lifecycle. This is a practical organizing framework rather than a universal standard.

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
Each part answers a different question. Instructions explain the task. State records where the work stands. Verification determines whether it works. Scope limits how much is attempted. Session handling makes the work resumable.

### Instructions: make the next action clear

Start with the goal, relevant repository conventions, and a concrete completion condition. Load detailed guidance when the task reaches the part of the system that needs it. A long instruction file can become difficult to maintain and can crowd out more useful context.

For example, this instruction gives an agent a behavior to verify:

```markdown
## Task
Add a retry action to the failed-upload state.

## Expected behavior
- Preserve the selected file after a network failure.
- Show the failure beside the upload control.
- Allow retry without selecting the file again.

## Verification
Simulate a failed request, retry it, and confirm that the file uploads once.
```

The expected behavior is specific enough for a reviewer to assess. It also leaves room for the agent to choose a suitable implementation instead of dictating unrelated details.

For more on selecting and maintaining useful context, see Anthropic’s [context engineering discussion](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents).

### State: record facts that survive a new session

Conversation history is useful, but it should not be the only place where a long task’s decisions live. Keep a small progress record with the current objective, completed work, verification evidence, and next action.

For a feature tracker, a record can be as simple as:

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
```json
{
  "id": "upload-retry",
  "status": "active",
  "expectedBehavior": "Retry the retained file after a failed upload",
  "checks": [],
  "nextAction": "Test the failed-request path in the browser"
}
```

Update the status from evidence. A feature should not become `passing` because the model predicts that its patch is correct.

Anthropic’s [long-running agent example](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) uses an initialization phase, incremental work, and persistent artifacts to bridge sessions. It is one implementation pattern; it does not establish that every project needs multiple agents.

### Verification: test the behavior at the right layer

A useful check should detect a failure that matters to the task. A compiler can catch a type mismatch, while a browser test can catch a button hidden behind an overlay. Neither replaces the other.

| Check | What it can establish | What it can miss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static checks | Syntax, types, selected code rules | Whether a user can finish the flow |
| Focused tests | Behavior under controlled inputs | Real configuration and wiring errors |
| Integration or browser checks | Connected behavior in an actual environment | Cases the flow did not exercise |

Choose checks according to the change. A copy edit does not need a large test suite. An authentication change needs more evidence than a successful build.

When a check fails, return a compact diagnostic: the command, failure, relevant location, and reproduction steps. Avoid attaching a guessed fix as if it were established fact.

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
```json
{
  "check": "upload retry flow",
  "result": "failed",
  "observed": "The retry request has no file body",
  "reproduce": [
    "Select a file",
    "Make the first request fail",
    "Click Retry"
  ]
}
```

This gives the next turn something observable to investigate.

### Scope: complete a useful slice

A task such as “finish the dashboard” leaves too many decisions open. A smaller slice—“show a recoverable empty state when the reports request fails”—has a clear trigger and outcome.

Work on one slice, verify it, then choose the next. Parallel work can help when changes are independent, but it also introduces coordination and integration costs. Add it when those costs are justified by the task.

Scope also belongs in the runtime. Bound model turns, tool calls, elapsed time, and output size. A retry should have a reason, a limit, and a stopping condition.

### Session lifecycle: leave a usable handoff

A new session should be able to answer three questions quickly: what is the goal, what is already true, and what should happen next?

```markdown
# Progress

## Goal
Make failed uploads recoverable without losing the selected file.

## Completed
- Added an error state and Retry control.
- Preserved the File object between attempts.

## Evidence
- Type check passed.
- Browser check: failed request followed by a successful retry.

## Next
Review the upload state when navigating away during a request.

## Open questions
- Should navigation cancel an in-flight upload?
```

A handoff is a compact record of the work, not a transcript of every command. Record a limitation when it matters to the next person.

## 3. Make the execution loop bounded

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
Keep the full artifact available, but pass a concise result back to the model: what ran, what changed, whether it passed, and where to read the details. Summaries should preserve failures and uncertainty rather than flatten them into “everything looks good.”

```text
Check: upload retry browser flow
Result: failed
Observed: second request contains no file body
Evidence: artifacts/upload-retry-trace.zip
Next: inspect how the request body is rebuilt on retry
```

Before a handoff, save decisions that would be expensive to rediscover. Do not store private user information merely because a persistent memory mechanism exists.

## 5. Adapt the workflow to local models

Local inference changes latency, memory limits, and model capability. It does not remove the need for clear tools and verification. Smaller tasks, concise tool results, and explicit state transitions can make the workflow easier to follow and inspect.

Treat this relay simulation as a metaphor for incremental work and handoffs. It is not a performance comparison between models or orchestration frameworks.

For structured output, use a supported schema mechanism where available, then validate the result in the application. Do not extract an arbitrary substring between braces and assume it is valid. Braces can appear inside strings, and syntactically valid JSON can still contain invalid actions.

If validation fails, return the specific schema error and allow a limited correction attempt. Repeated failures should end the run with a clear explanation.

## 6. Start with a small repository contract

A short repository guide can describe the environment without trying to encode every possible decision:

```markdown
# Repository guide

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
## Environment
- Use the package manager and lockfile already in the repository.
- Read the relevant module before changing its public interface.

## Work
- Define the user-visible outcome before editing.
- Keep unrelated changes out of the task.
- Follow the existing component and styling conventions.

## Finish
- Run checks appropriate to the behavior that changed.
- Report what passed, what failed, and what was not checked.
- Leave a short handoff if work remains.
```

Enforce critical boundaries in tools and runtime policy. An instruction file is helpful guidance, but it cannot substitute for operating-system permissions, schema validation, or an execution budget.

## 7. Measure whether the harness helps

Choose a repeatable set of tasks and compare outcomes under the same conditions. Record completion against observable acceptance criteria, time to a useful result, tool failures, and interventions needed to recover.

Inspect unsuccessful runs as carefully as successful ones. Did retrieval miss a file? Did a command fail? Did the model misunderstand the task? Did the verification exercise the wrong behavior? Each answer points to a different change.

Avoid attributing every failure to the harness or every improvement to the model. Both matter, and results from one benchmark do not automatically transfer to a different repository or task.

## What I would build first

Start with a single bounded loop, a small set of tools, a durable progress record, and a verification step that exercises the intended behavior. Add routing, delegation, and more elaborate memory only when a concrete failure calls for them.

title: Harness Engineering: Building Reliable AI Agents
content:
The aim is a workflow that can explain its progress and recover from mistakes. A useful harness makes it easier to see why the agent succeeded—and easier to fix the system when it did not.

## Further reading

- [Building effective agents — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)

title: LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
content:
A useful AI application does more than send a question to a model. It gathers the right information, keeps provider credentials on the server, and gives the user a sensible outcome when a dependency is slow or unavailable.

LangChain provides composable interfaces for parts of that work. I find it most useful when a request has several meaningful steps: prepare a prompt, retrieve evidence, call a model, and process the result. For a single straightforward model call, a provider SDK may be enough.

This guide starts with a small TypeScript pipeline and expands it into retrieval-augmented generation, or **RAG**. It also explains where LangGraph and the Vercel AI SDK fit, so that each library has a clear job.

> Follow the data through the application before choosing an abstraction. Knowing what enters and leaves each step makes both debugging and deployment easier.

## 1. Give each part of the stack a job

| Part | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Next.js | Application routes, server boundaries, and the React interface |
| Groq | Hosted inference for a supported model |
| LangChain | Model interfaces, prompts, retrieval, and composable operations |
| LangGraph | Explicit state and control flow for workflows that need it |
| Vercel AI SDK | Model and UI streaming utilities, transports, and React chat state |
| A document store | Persist the source material and retrieval metadata |

You do not need every part for every project. In particular, a fixed retrieve-then-answer pipeline does not require an agent that decides which tool to call next.

title: LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
content:
The examples below use TypeScript and server-side environment variables. Pin compatible package versions in a real project; the AI SDK integration section uses the current adapter API and should not be mixed directly with older SDK-major examples.

## 2. Start with one inspectable model call

Install the core interfaces and the provider integration:

```bash
npm install @langchain/core @langchain/groq
```

Set `GROQ_API_KEY` on the server and set `GROQ_MODEL` to a model available to your account. Keeping the model name in configuration makes it easier to change a provider-specific choice without editing application logic.

```typescript

const modelName = process.env.GROQ_MODEL;
if (!modelName) throw new Error("Set GROQ_MODEL before running this example");

const model = new ChatGroq({
  model: modelName,
  temperature: 0,
  maxTokens: 400,
  maxRetries: 1,
});

const reply = await model.invoke([
  ["system", "Explain technical ideas clearly and briefly."],
  ["human", "What problem does a retriever solve?"],
]);

console.log(reply.content);
```

The result is a message object. Its content is not the same thing as an HTTP response or a UI streaming protocol. The [ChatGroq integration reference](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/integrations/chat/groq) documents the provider-specific options and supported features.

Keep API keys out of client components and public environment variables. Browser users should call your application route rather than receiving the provider credential.

## 3. Compose a prompt, model, and parser

A prompt template separates stable instructions from request-specific values. A runnable pipeline connects operations whose inputs and outputs fit together.

```typescript

LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
content:
## 6. Use LangGraph when the control flow needs state

A linear pipeline is easy to inspect. More complex workflows may need branches, retries, checkpoints, or a pause for human input. [LangGraph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/langgraph/overview) provides primitives for explicitly modeling that state and control flow.

For example, a workflow might route based on retrieval quality:

```text
Receive question
  → Retrieve passages
  → Check whether evidence is sufficient
      → Yes: generate an answer with source references
      → No: ask a clarifying question
  → Save the relevant conversation state
```

Be precise about what “evidence is sufficient” means. It might involve deterministic filters, a measured similarity threshold, or a separate evaluation step. Do not assume a model’s self-assigned confidence is calibrated.

A checkpoint records execution state. Conversation history records messages. A vector store holds searchable material. They solve different problems and have different retention requirements.

## 7. Connect streaming to the browser deliberately

A stream of text chunks and a stream of structured chat events are different protocols. The browser transport and server response must agree on which one they exchange.

For current AI SDK integrations, the [LangChain adapter](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/adapters/langchain) provides message and stream conversion utilities in `@ai-sdk/langchain`. Use its documented UI message conversion with a compatible AI SDK version. Older examples importing `LangChainAdapter` directly from `ai` belong to earlier APIs.

title: LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
content:
| Server output | Matching client behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Plain text stream | Read and decode text chunks with a compatible fetch client |
| AI SDK UI message stream | Use the matching AI SDK chat transport and UI state |
| JSON response | Parse JSON and render the returned fields |

In Next.js App Router, `app/api/chat/route.ts` normally exposes `/api/chat`. The filename `route.ts` is not part of the browser URL.

Streaming improves the time until something useful is visible. It does not remove retrieval latency or prevent a later failure. Show an honest pending state, provide a retry path, and preserve the user’s question when the request fails.

## 8. Design the first failed request

Before deployment, decide what the user should see if the document service is cold, retrieval returns no match, or the model provider is unavailable. Treat these as expected system states rather than surprising exceptions.

- Put deadlines around external work and inside the hosting platform’s request limit.
- Keep a small local answer path for essential, already-published facts when that fits the product.
- Distinguish an empty search result from an unavailable service.
- Limit input size and retained history so one request cannot grow without bound.
- Keep raw provider errors in operational logs; give users a clear next action.

A fallback should have a defined scope. Returning an unrelated generic answer can conceal a failure and reduce trust just as much as an error screen.

## 9. Evaluate the whole answer path

Use a small, repeatable question set before changing prompts or retrieval settings. Include direct questions, paraphrases, missing information, unrelated questions, and requests that refer to an earlier message.

title: LangChain in TypeScript: From Model Calls to Reliable RAG
content:
For each case, inspect the retrieved passages, whether the answer is supported, whether citations identify the actual evidence, and how long the user waits. Add a dependency-outage case as well: a good answer path should have an understandable failure path.

Keep model choice, document set, and test inputs fixed when comparing a change. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to tell which part caused the difference.

## A practical starting point

Begin with one model call that you can inspect. Add a prompt and parser when they make the data flow clearer. Add retrieval when the answer needs your own material. Add explicit graph state when branching and resumability justify it.

The useful outcome is a request path you can explain: where the evidence came from, how the model used it, what the browser received, and how the application behaves when any step fails.

## Further reading

- [ChatGroq integration — LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/integrations/chat/groq)
- [Retrieval — LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/langchain/retrieval)
- [LangGraph overview — LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/langgraph/overview)
- [LangChain adapter — Vercel AI SDK](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/adapters/langchain)
